links.note: The two quotations at the start of the chapter are Tagore on the touch of the One in the play of the many and Sri Aurobindo on unity in diversity, the Many in the One - both are in this concept, which is where they open the chapter.

Selecting Panchatantra stories and discussing whether their message still holds - this concept is the Panchatantra, a collection of stories with animals as the main characters that teaches important life skills.
Collecting a few folk tales from your region and discussing their message is verbatim one of this concept's closing questions, and it is not tied to any single text the chapter treats.
Any ancient story seen depicted through a sculpture, a painting, a dance performance or a movie is verbatim the last of this concept's closing questions.

Nehru's observation that illiterate villagers knew hundreds of verses by heart and that the epics were engraved on the popular mind - this concept carries that quotation in full. Already linked and correct.
What unity in diversity signifies - this concept names the principle in Sri Aurobindo's words, the Many in the One, and states the chapter's thesis before any evidence is offered.
The People of India project counting 325 languages across 4,635 communities - this concept's figures. Already linked and correct.

Vincent Smith wondering how a history of India could be written in the face of such bewildering diversity, and the chapter's answer that India offers unity in diversity - this concept's passage. Already linked and correct.
The sari as a plain length of cloth, unstitched - this concept's description of it, which is what the whole unity-and-diversity argument about clothing rests on.
Ruling out Egyptian Cotton against Banarasi, Kanjivaram and Patan Patola is decided against this concept's list of famous silk saris.
Hundreds of varieties of sari differing in weave, design and colour - this concept's account of how one unstitched cloth becomes many. Already linked and correct.
The stone relief from Vaishali, today in Bihar, going back a few centuries BCE - this concept's dating evidence for the sari, with relief glossed alongside.
Chintz, the printed cotton so popular in 17th-century Europe that England and France banned its import - this concept's DON'T MISS OUT box.
New ways of draping the sari still being invented - this concept states it, alongside the many regional and community ways of wearing the same single dress.
The sari put to many uses beyond that of a dress, with six pictures of such creative uses - this concept's LET'S EXPLORE.
Pongal as the Tamil Nadu name of the harvest festival - this concept is the Makara Sankranti map of the different names of similar festivals across India at about the same date.
Magh Bihu of Assam among the names for the festival celebrated around Makara Sankranti - this concept's map. Already linked and correct.
About 200 adaptations of the Panchatantra in more than 50 languages - this concept's estimate, and its point that one collection of stories has become many.
The Ramayana and the Mahabharata as the two Sanskrit epics whose heroes fight to re-establish dharma - this concept's opening. Already linked and correct.
The Pandavas fighting their own cousins the Kauravas to recover their kingdom - this concept's summary of the Mahabharata. Already linked and correct.
Ravana, the demon who kidnapped Sita - this concept's summary of the Ramayana. Already linked and correct.
The countless folk versions and tribal adaptations of the two epics - this concept gathers them, including the hundred folk Mahabharatas counted in Tamil Nadu alone. Already linked and correct.
The Bhils, the Gonds and the Mundas named among the tribal communities with their own versions of the epics - this concept's list. Already linked and correct.
Pigments as the substances that give colour - this concept mentions the endless variations in colour produced from many kinds of pigments.
Pairing Magh Bihu with Assam against Pongal, Lohri and Uttarayan - all four names come from this concept's map of the same festival across India.

Diversity celebrated as an enrichment rather than a division - this concept's summary says India's unity celebrates diversity because diversity does not divide, it enriches, which is exactly the assertion.
The false option claims the sari is worn in one style; this concept states that there are many ways of wearing it, varying by region and community, and that new ways are still being invented.

The visible statement about the dhoti as another unstitched garment matches this concept's LET'S EXPLORE, which asks the reader to list the styles and uses of the dhoti following the example of the sari. The item's other numbered statements are missing from the stem.
An epic glossed as a long poem narrating the adventures of heroes and great figures of the past - this concept's definition. Already linked and correct.
Tribal legends on how the Pandavas and Draupadi visited their regions - this concept's account, which is what the shared-heritage inference rests on. Already linked and correct.
The 25 scripts counted by the People of India project - that figure is in this concept, beside the 325 languages.
Patan Patola as the silk sari of Patan in Gujarat - this concept names it among the famous types of silk sari, with Banarasi, Kanjivaram and Muga as the other options.

The Panchatantra adapted into almost every Indian language and travelling to Southeast Asia, the Arab world and Europe - this concept's account, and the reason given is the life skills its stories teach.

Spotting Magh Bihu as not a Punjab festival is decided against this concept's map of the names of the harvest festival across India, which is where Uttarayan, Pongal, Magh Bihu and Lohri all come from.
Staple grains as the basic food for most Indians - this concept's definition after listing the cereals, millets and pulses. Already linked and correct.

Indian textiles sought after in 17th-century Europe - this concept states that India produced the finest cotton in the world and that chintz was popular enough for England and France to ban it. Already linked and correct.
